1	# Task dispatch without slots — the work-item queue
2	
3	The mechanism lives in [`engine/scheduler/queue/`](../../engine/scheduler/queue/),
4	behind `taskScheduler.dispatch`. A continuation of the owner's sketch (2026-08-12, reproduced in Appendix A), played against twenty timed
5	scenarios ([SCENARIOS.md](SCENARIOS.md)) and the field's prior art
6	([RESEARCH.md](RESEARCH.md)), with the owner's eight decisions of 2026-08-13
7	recorded in §15 and folded into the sections they changed. The phase plan
8	belongs to a tracking issue, not here. It supersedes
9	the slot machinery of
10	[per-project-scheduling DESIGN §3–§5](../per-project-scheduling/DESIGN.md) and
11	amends several of its §12 decisions (each amendment is named where it happens).
12	What it does **not** touch: the task folder anatomy (§1), the precondition
13	contract, code-work and its secrets model
14	([task-code-work DESIGN](../task-code-work/DESIGN.md)), the outcome ceiling, the
15	security posture (the issue is data; behavior comes from tracked files), and the
16	usage-metrics records.
17	
18	The shape in one paragraph: **work items are issues, available for work; any
19	number of executors pull from them.** A thin generator tick gives every
20	recurring task a standing work item at its anchor and flips blocked items
21	ready — pure label mechanics, no preconditions, no signals. An executor — a
22	GitHub Action by default, but anything that can read issues — picks up the
23	next ready item, claims it by label, evaluates the precondition (the only
24	place it ever runs): on a go it runs the work step and hands off to agentic work (a
25	CCR session invoked by API); on a no-go the item **rolls** — stamped
26	not-before the task's next anchor, blocked, reason recorded — so the item
27	itself carries "asked, declined, wakes at T". Follow-ups, fan-outs, urgency,
28	and one-off forcing are all just *creating or waking work items*. There is no
29	slot id, no run-ledger watermark, no exclusive claim, and no label-event
30	re-arm.
31	
32	---
33	
34	## 1. What the slot machinery costs today
35	
36	The current design is push-shaped: one hourly scheduler run decides, at a single
37	instant, everything that will happen — which tasks are due, whether they run,
38	what they may touch — and encodes the decision into dispatch issues that a
39	label-event-triggered session then executes. Every complication below is a
40	consequence of that shape.
41	
42	- **The slot id is state smuggled into a title token.** `d2026-08-12`,
43	  `h2026-08-12T14Z`, `m2026-08` exist so that a scheduled occurrence has an
44	  identity — which the exactly-once guard needs (title search per slot), the
45	  stale backstop needs (the *leading character* of the slot id is parsed back
46	  into a period, `SLOT_PERIOD_MS`), and forcing needs (the `~f<runId>` marker
47	  appended so an operator re-run of an already-run slot isn't silently
48	  swallowed). Three mechanisms each decode a fragment of scheduler state out of
49	  a string in an issue title.
50	
51	- **Due-ness lives in a platform side channel.** "Has this slot run?" is
52	  answered by the Actions run ledger of the scheduler workflow itself
53	  (`lastSuccessTime`) — a watermark that is not visible beside the work, must
54	  exclude forced runs to stay correct, and whose unreadability has to fail the
55	  whole run (an exit-0 abort would advance it past slots it never evaluated).
56	  The state the system actually cares about — *was this occurrence's work
57	  created?* — is derivable from the issues themselves, and nothing reads it
58	  from there. *(A first cut of the go/no-go ruling briefly reintroduced a
59	  ledger read; the standing-item model (§5) removed it again — the tick is
60	  now a pure function of the clock and the issue list.)*
61	
62	- **A decision made at one instant cannot express ordering, only simultaneity.**
63	  The nightly chain's ordering is faked by anchor-hour staggering, which
64	  collapses whenever GitHub fires the cron late — hence the `exclusive: true`
65	  claim, a task-level hack whose cost is real: **a deferred slot is spent, not
66	  queued**, so a claim on the wrong night silently halves throughput. The
67	  system has no way to say "run B after A"; it can only say "run A alone".
68	
69	- **Label-event invocation is lossy, and the loss shaped three mechanisms.**
70	  The executor routine fires only on a fresh `labeled` event; a lost delivery
71	  leaves an armed issue sitting forever. So: the janitor's re-arm
72	  (remove/re-add the label to emit a new event), the 20-minute grace window so
73	  a re-arm never hands a live session a rival, and the stale escalation that
74	  bounds the re-arm loop. The claim protocol then has to survive *duplicate*
75	  events (the read-swap-confirm lease). All of it is compensation for a trigger
76	  that neither confirms delivery nor can be polled.
77	
78	- **Capacity, urgency, and follow-ups have no home.** There is exactly one
79	  implicit executor per repo and no way to add another; nothing distinguishes
80	  urgent work from routine work; a task cannot schedule a successor ("validate
81	  in two days what tonight's run delivered") except by hoping a future
82	  precondition rediscovers the situation. Forcing (`FORCE_TASKS`) is a special
83	  engine path with its own exemptions (skips preconditions, exempt from
84	  deferral, excluded from the watermark, slot-id marker) — where "run this now"
85	  ought to be the system's most ordinary operation.
86	
87	- **Visibility is split three ways.** Whether something *will* run is ledger
88	  math nobody can see; whether it *is* running is labels on an issue; what it
89	  *did* is a record line in a captured transcript. There is no one place where
90	  the state of the repo's recurring work can be read.
91	
92	What is worth keeping — and this design keeps all of it — is everything the
93	incidents taught: one session executes exactly one item and never sweeps the
94	queue (the duplicate-execution bug, DESIGN §5), the claim is a verified lease,
95	the issue is data and never instructions, behavior-defining content comes only
96	from tracked files, every exit converges to one visible terminal state, and
97	recovery lives in one place, in code.
98	
99	## 2. The shape — a pull-based queue of work items
100	
101	Four roles, strictly separated (this refines, rather than replaces, the
102	2026-08-06 three-responsibility split — the scheduler's job splits in two and
103	shrinks):
104	
105	1. **The generator** — a thin scheduled tick (the repo's one cron, unchanged
106	   rule). Three jobs, all deterministic label mechanics over the issue list:
107	   *instantiate* each recurring task's standing item when its time comes,
108	   *ready* blocked items whose dependencies have resolved and whose not-before
109	   has passed, and *reclaim* dead executor claims. It evaluates no
110	   preconditions and collects no signals (§5); it executes nothing.
111	2. **Executors** — any number of pull workers. Each iteration: pick the next
112	   ready item (urgent first), claim it, evaluate the precondition — the only
113	   place it is ever evaluated — then on a go run the work step and either finish
114	   (agentless task) or invoke the agentic phase and hand the item to it; on a
115	   no-go, roll a scheduled item to its next anchor (§5). An executor is
116	   platform-agnostic by construction: its whole interface is issue read/write
117	   plus the repo at HEAD. More capacity = more executors.
118	3. **Agents** — CCR sessions, one per handed-off item, invoked by the executor.
119	   An agent executes its one item's task file, verifies its outcome ceiling,
120	   and converges the item to a terminal state.
121	4. **The janitor** — unchanged in role, smaller in scope: dead executor claims,
122	   dead agent claims, stale-item escalation, queue health review. The re-arm
123	   retires (§11).
124	
125	The queue itself is the repo's issues, and under the standing-item model that
126	sentence is complete: everything the system knows — including "this task was
127	asked, declined, and wakes again at T" — is on a work item. No plan file, no
128	watermark, no ledger read. The tick is a pure function of the clock and the
129	issue list; which is what the sketch means by *visibility into state*.
130	
131	## 3. The work item
132	
133	An issue, `[claudinite-work] <pack>/<task>` (plus an optional free-form
134	qualifier after the task, for tasks that legitimately have several concurrent
135	items — a fan-out names its target: `[claudinite-work] sheepdog/fleet-baseline
136	member-repo-x`). **The issue number is the identity.** No slot id: an
137	occurrence needs no name beyond the item that embodies it, and everything the
138	slot id encoded is recovered elsewhere — dedup from the family's creation
139	timestamps (§5), staleness from the task's own declared frequency read at HEAD
140	(§11), forcing from the fact that creating an item *is* forcing (§8).
141	
142	Body, machine-first (same parsing discipline as today's dispatch body — the
143	first line is the task path, validated in code before anything trusts it):
144	
145	```
146	.claudinite/shared/packs/basics/tasks/baselining/task.md
147	
148	Not-before: 2026-08-14T04:00Z            # optional — see §9
149	Blocked-by: #812, #813                   # optional — see §9
150	
151	Execute the Claudinite task above.
152	The Context section below is binding scope — do not re-decide it.
153	
154	### Context
155	- <the creating precondition's binding lines, verbatim — unchanged>
156	
157	### Delivered by code-work
158	- <written by the executor at hand-off, unchanged shape>
159	```
160	
161	Everything behavior-defining — model, outcome ceiling, worker content, the
162	work step's command — is still read from the tracked task files at HEAD, never from the
163	issue. A work item whose task the repo no longer carries is closed as obsolete,
164	exactly like today's exit-14.
165	
166	**Standing vs ad-hoc is structural — there is no origin marker** (owner,
167	2026-08-19; this deletes `origin:schedule`, and `origin:request` dies unbuilt).
168	An **unqualified** item of a task with a frequency *is* that task's standing
169	item: the guards (§5) key on the bare title and the frequency read at HEAD, so
170	nothing is hand-classified. Everything else is ad-hoc — an item of a `manual`
171	task, or any item carrying a qualifier — and sits outside the family by its
172	very title, so scheduled work and ad-hoc work never suppress each other: a
173	pending follow-up (its own task) does not silence tomorrow's occurrence, and a
174	fan-out target (qualified) does not consume it. Two consequences, both
175	deliberate: creating an unqualified item of a scheduled task where none is
176	open **is** minting its standing item — the same act as §8's force lever, not
177	a lookalike — so deliberate concurrency for one task always names a qualifier;
178	and a request item needs no marker either, being known by its `Request:` field
179	(§16.3). The fielded engine still applies `origin:schedule` until the
180	vocabulary migration; the label becomes inert stored data the decoders ignore.
181	A task whose precondition should care about open follow-ups can see them
182	through the `issues` signal, as task-specific logic where it belongs.
183	
184	## 4. The state machine
185	
186	```
187	                     ┌────────────► closed  task:obsolete
188	                     │                    (precondition no longer holds; task gone)
189	 created ─► task:blocked ─► task:ready ─► task:executing ─► task:agent ─► closed  task:done
190	            (only when       (queue)       (claimed by an     (handed to        open    needs-human
191	             Blocked-by /                   executor)          a CCR session)           + one of the four
192	             Not-before                                                                   triage sub-labels
193	             present)
194	```
195	
196	Labels, the full vocabulary:
197	
198	| label | means | applied by |
199	|---|---|---|
200	| `task:blocked` | waiting on `Blocked-by` issues and/or `Not-before` | creator |
201	| `task:ready` | available for pickup | creator or the tick |
202	| `task:urgent` | modifier: pick before any non-urgent item | creator (write-gated, like every label) |
203	| `task:executing` | an executor holds the claim | executor, on claim |
204	| `task:agent` | an agent session owns it | executor, at hand-off |
205	| `task:done` | succeeded; nothing pending (closed) | executor or agent |
206	| `outcome:delivered` | **retired 2026-08-19, still read.** Meant "succeeded and left a live artifact the world still has to act on"; an unmerged PR now parks at `task:needs-human-approval` instead of closing, and nothing else ever wrote it. Closed issues carrying it are stored data, so every decoder still recognises it | — (historical) |
207	| `task:obsolete` | never ran: the pickup-time precondition said no, or the task is gone from the repo (closed as not planned) | executor |
208	| `needs-human` | parked for a human — the one triage *state*, and what every guard, sweep and dashboard turns on (open) | anyone, incl. janitor |
209	| `task:needs-human-action` | …and something outside the code must change first: a secret set, a scope granted, a routine rewired, an input supplied | anyone, incl. janitor |
210	| `task:needs-human-decision` | …and the run stopped mid-flight, so the next step is a choice: re-queue or abandon, does the half-done work stand, was the ceiling violation acceptable | anyone, incl. janitor |
211	| `task:needs-human-approval` | …and it **succeeded**, deliberately leaving an unmerged PR. The one park that is not a fault | executor or agent |
212	| `task:needs-human-failure` | …and the run broke: a bug, a contract-forbidden shape, a malformed or forged item. The default when nothing else fits | anyone, incl. janitor |
213	
214	**The terminal labels live in the `task:` namespace** (owner, 2026-08-19):
215	`task:done` and `task:obsolete` — one vocabulary for the state machine's live
216	*and* terminal states, and the `outcome:` namespace dissolves. The fielded
217	engine writes the old spellings (`outcome:done`, `outcome:obsolete`) until the
218	vocabulary migration lands; per the stored-data rename rule, decoders map
219	every legacy spelling straight to today's, and `outcome:delivered` — which
220	nothing writes — stays a recognized legacy spelling forever.
221	
222	**Every park wears two labels**: `needs-human` *and* exactly one sub-label. The
223	state and the routing are different questions — the machine reads the first, a
224	person reads the second — and collapsing them would have meant a migration to
225	land rather than an additive write (the collapse is #1050's, once the fleet has
226	converged past the split).
227	
228	**A park wearing no sub-label reads as `failure`.** That is the compatibility
229	direction chosen deliberately: every item an engine older than the split left
230	behind, and every kind word a newer engine invents that this one does not know,
231	holds the lane rather than silently letting a broken task keep filing work.
232	
233	**Only a `failure` park holds the task's lane** (§5). An open unqualified item
234	of a scheduled task *is* its standing item (§3), so while one exists no further
235	occurrence is filed — for a break that is the point, since a queue of items that will fail the
236	same way helps nobody and the silence is the signal. For the other three it is a
237	bug: a PR waiting on a reviewer, a decision waiting on its owner and a secret
238	waiting to be set are one person's inbox, not a fault in the task, and #1032
239	measured what conflating them costs — a permission gap parked `missingbulb/Shepherd`'s
240	`fleet-digest` for two days while its dashboard read healthy, because no item was
241	ever filed behind the parked one. So the generator drops non-blocking parks from
242	both the standing-item test and the duplicate sweep beside it.
243	
244	This is the sketch's lifecycle with two adjustments, both argued for rather
245	than assumed:
246	
247	- **Executor identity is a claim comment, not a label.** The sketch's
248	  `being-handled-by-executor-1` puts an unbounded set (executor identities) into
249	  a vocabulary that must stay small and queryable; every new executor would mint
250	  a label, and a query for "what is executing" would have to know every
251	  executor's name. One state label (`task:executing`) answers the query; the
252	  claim comment — which the lease protocol requires anyway — carries *who*
253	  (executor id, run URL) and *when*. Same for `task:agent`: the hand-off
254	  comment names the CCR session.
255	- **`succeeded-with-unexpected-result` became `outcome:delivered`, and then
256	  became a park.** "Unexpected" would blur two things that must not blur: a run
257	  that legitimately left a pending artifact within its ceiling (open-pr task →
258	  open PR: *expected*, but the world hasn't finished with it), and a run that
259	  violated its ceiling (a `none` task that opened a PR). The second is still a
260	  **failure**, now `task:needs-human-decision` — someone must say whether the
261	  overreach stands — exactly as `verify-outcome` enforces. The first turned out
262	  not to be a terminal state at all: a PR nobody has merged is waiting on a
263	  named person, and closing the item hid that from every surface that counts
264	  open work, so it parks at `task:needs-human-approval` and stays open. It does
265	  not hold the lane, so the reviewer's silence delays only the review.
266	
267	Terminal-state discipline is unchanged: every item converges exactly once to
268	exactly one end — one of the two closes, or a park under one of the four
269	sub-labels — with one comment saying what happened.
270	
271	**Label writes are granular, always** ([RESEARCH](RESEARCH.md) §2): add and
272	remove named labels (REST POST/DELETE), never write the label *set* (PUT,
273	GraphQL `updateIssue`) — a set-write replaces from a stale snapshot and
274	clobbers concurrent transitions, a bug class GitHub's own CLI shipped
275	([cli/cli#4861](https://github.com/cli/cli/pull/4861)). With multiple
276	executors and a tick all moving labels, this is a correctness rule, not a
277	style preference.
278	
279	**The road back from `needs-human`** (SCENARIOS S12/S19, F7): a human who has
280	resolved the cause re-queues the item by removing `needs-human` and its
281	sub-label and applying `task:ready` — the sanctioned retry lever, write-gated like every label
282	operation here. The next pickup re-runs the precondition (§6.4), which is what
283	makes the retry safe even when the failed run half-did its work. Alternatively
284	the human closes the item (optionally superseding it with a forced retry,
285	§8); nothing mechanical ever re-queues a `needs-human` item.
286	
287	## 5. The generator — the standing work item
288	
289	> Amended 2026-08-18 (§16.3): the tick has a **fourth** job, `adopt` — an ordinary
290	> issue marked `claude-task` becomes a work item, and the mark is consumed in the
291	> same pass. It is the same kind of job as the other three: label mechanics over
292	> the issue list, no precondition, no signal.
293	
294	**The tick never evaluates a precondition and never collects a signal**
295	(owner model, 2026-08-13). Creation is calendar-only: at a task's anchor, the
296	tick creates its work item *unconditionally* — the precondition speaks later,
297	at pickup, on the executor (§6.4), which is where the original sketch had it
298	all along. What happens on a no-go is the model's whole trick: the item is
299	**not closed** — the executor stamps it `Not-before: <the task's next anchor>`,
300	swaps it back to `task:blocked`, records the reason, and the item **rolls
301	forward**. The next anchor readies it again; the next pick re-asks. One ask
302	per period, exactly — go/no-go preserved — and the memory of "evaluated,
303	declined, ask again at T" is carried **on the item itself**, in the one place
304	this design keeps state.
305	
306	```text
307	tick(now):
308	  if dormant: return                            # before any read, as today
309	
310	  # ---- job 1: instantiate (calendar-only; no preconditions, no signals) ----
311	  for task in discoverTasks():                  # NO ordering requirement — the
312	    if task.frequency == 'manual': continue     # `after` yield is pick-time (§6.1)
313	    A = mostRecentAnchor(task.frequency, config.taskScheduler, now)
314	    family = issues(title == "[claudinite-work] <pack>/<task>", state ALL)
315	                    # the exact bare title — a qualified item is outside the
316	                    # family structurally (§3), no marker involved
317	                    # REST issue list, never the search index (S6/F11)
318	    # A park that is somebody's INBOX rather than a fault does not hold the
319	    # lane: it is neither the standing item nor a duplicate of one, so it drops
320	    # out of the two OPEN tests below and the schedule goes on around it. A
321	    # `failure` park, and any park an older engine left unclassified, stays in
322	    # (§4). It stays in `family` for the occurrence guard further down, which is
323	    # the point: the parked item DID consume its own occurrence, so the next
324	    # item is filed at the next anchor and not immediately.
325	    live = [i for i in family if not (i has "needs-human" and not blockingPark(i))]
326	    # F16 self-heal first: nothing documents that a REST list from another
327	    # node sees a creation seconds old, so a stale list can let a duplicate
328	    # standing item through. Assume it will happen rather than that it won't:
329	    # close every open family item but the OLDEST, task:obsolete, with a
330	    # dedupe comment. Serialized by the tick's concurrency group.
331	    if count(i.state == OPEN for i in live) > 1: closeAllButOldest(live)
332	    if any(i.state == OPEN for i in live):      continue  # the standing item
333	                                                          # already exists
334	    # the occurrence guard has TWO halves (F13, caught by the simulator): an
335	    # item CREATED at-or-after A covers this occurrence — and so does an item
336	    # CLOSED at-or-after A, because a rolled item created in an earlier
337	    # period that ran and closed today consumed today's occurrence. With the
338	    # created_at half alone, the very next tick after such a close creates a
339	    # second item for the same occurrence: a double execution.
340	    if any(i.created_at >= A or i.closed_at >= A for i in family): continue
341	    createIssue(title:  "[claudinite-work] <pack>/<task>",
342	                body:   taskPath,
343	                labels: [family.isEmpty ? "task:blocked" : "task:ready"])
344	                # a brand-new task's FIRST item is born blocked with
345	                # Not-before = its next anchor — adoption must not fire
346	                # weekly/monthly tasks off-anchor (the old first-run concern)
347	
348	  # ---- job 2: ready whatever is due --------------------------------------
349	  for item in issues(label "task:blocked", state OPEN):   # any origin
350	    {blockedBy, notBefore} = parseBody(item)
351	    if all(issues(blockedBy).state == CLOSED) and now >= notBefore:
352	      swapLabel(item, "task:blocked" -> "task:ready")
353	
354	  # ---- job 3: reclaim dead executor claims (§11) --------------------------
355	  for item in issues(label "task:executing", state OPEN):
356	    if noActivitySince(item, EXECUTING_LEASH): stripToReady(item, comment)
357	```
358	
359	And the roll, executor-side (the full pick flow is §6):
360	
361	```text
362	on pick, verdict = precondition(signals, config):
363	  go     -> proceed (work step, hand-off, converge, CLOSE with an outcome)
364	  no-go  -> item is the task's standing item (§3 — unqualified, frequency at HEAD)?
365	              yes: Not-before = nextAnchor(task.frequency); ready -> blocked;
366	                   record the reason            # the item ROLLS — not an exit
367	              no:  close task:obsolete          # ad-hoc (manual task, or
368	                                                # qualified): no anchor to roll to (S17)
369	```
370	
371	**What this dissolves, all at once:**
372	
373	- **The evaluate-once ledger.** No `lastTick`, no Actions-ledger read, no
374	  grace fallback: "was this occurrence evaluated" is answered by the standing
375	  item's own `Not-before`. §1's side-channel complaint is fully satisfied
376	  again — the tick is a pure function of the clock and the issue list.
377	- **The 24-attempts cost (F10).** The tick evaluates nothing; the precondition
378	  runs once per wake, i.e. once per period per task. Signals are collected by
379	  the executor for the one picked task — the tick performs no GitHub reads
380	  beyond the issue list.
381	- **Declined occurrences were invisible in every earlier model** — no-go
382	  meant no item (or a ledger entry nobody sees). Now a quiet task's item shows
383	  its last ask, its reason, and its next wake, on its timeline. This closes
384	  the last gap in the sketch's *visibility into state*.
385	- **Forcing needs no item creation in the common case** (§8): the standing
386	  item exists, so force = wake it — strip `task:blocked`, clear `Not-before`,
387	  optionally add `task:urgent`. The same lever as the human re-queue (§4),
388	  which is no accident.
389	- **F9 (topological creation order) retires unbuilt**: `after` no longer
390	  wires `Blocked-by` at creation — see §6.1/§9 — so the tick's iteration
391	  order stops mattering.
392	
393	**Titles carry no timestamp, and never will** (owner question, answered
394	plainly): every item of a task shares the bare title `[claudinite-work]
395	<pack>/<task>`; successive items are told apart by issue number, which is the
396	identity (§3). The optional qualifier exists only for deliberately concurrent
397	items (fan-out targets). Nothing ever parses a date out of a title — that was
398	the slot grammar, and it stays dead.
399	
400	**The costs, named:**
401	
402	- **The issue list's baseline changes meaning.** A quiet repo used to show
403	  zero open scheduler issues; now it shows one open (blocked) item per
404	  scheduled task, each stating its next wake. That is ~a dozen standing open
405	  issues here — read it as the dashboard it is: the issue list *is* the
406	  scheduler's state, which is what the sketch asked for. Filtering them out
407	  of "real issues" views is a title query — every work item wears the
408	  `[claudinite-work]` title prefix.
409	- **Hourly tasks churn their item.** An hourly task that stays no-go rolls
410	  ~24 times a day: two label flips and a body edit per roll, on one issue.
411	  Cheap against API quotas, noisy on that item's timeline; the roll writes no
412	  comment (the `Not-before` bump is the record) so the noise is timeline
413	  events, not comment spam. Named and accepted — one issue absorbs it.
414	- **A long-quiet task's item lives for months.** That is the feature wearing
415	  its cost: the item is the task's standing status line, and its age is
416	  information ("quiet since June"), not staleness — the janitor's stale rule
417	  keys on `task:ready` age, which a properly rolling item never accumulates.
418	
419	**Errored and forced items against the guards** (unchanged in substance from
420	the earlier draft, restated for the new shape):
421	
422	- A **failed run** parks its item open + `needs-human` (a real exit — the
423	  roll is only for no-go verdicts, never for failures). A `failure` park *is*
424	  the backlog guard: no new item until a human closes or re-queues it — one
425	  broken task, one triage item, however long it takes. The other three
426	  sub-labels are **not** guards (§4): a park that only wants a reviewer, a
427	  decision or a secret leaves the lane open, so the next occurrence is filed
428	  beside it on schedule. It still consumes its own occurrence, so nothing is
429	  filed until that next anchor.
430	- A **forced ad-hoc item** (qualified, or a manual task's — §3) is invisible
431	  to both guards in both directions, whatever state it ends in — its title is
432	  outside the family, so it neither suppresses nor consumes an occurrence
433	  (#749's property, now structural). An **unqualified** item of a scheduled
434	  task is never ad-hoc: creating one where none is open is minting the
435	  standing item (§8), and beside an open one it is a duplicate the F16
436	  self-heal closes.
437	- **Force-of-a-scheduled-task** is now the wake lever, not an item (§8), so
438	  the S15 same-title collision cannot arise from the common force at all; the
439	  pick mutex (§6.1) still covers a deliberately created concurrent item.
440	
441	## 6. The executor — pick up, claim, prepare, hand off
442	
443	An executor iteration, in code end to end (the reference implementation is a
444	job in the vendored workflow, triggered by `issues: labeled [task:ready]`
445	events for latency **and** by the tick's cron as the poll that makes lost
446	events irrelevant; `workflow_dispatch` for a hand-started drain):
447	
448	1. **Pick**: list open `task:ready` items; `task:urgent` first, then
449	   **random order among the ready** (owner decision, 2026-08-15). Two
450	   executors listing the same queue then contend on *different* heads
451	   instead of cascading down one — and nothing leans on oldest-first: the
452	   stale-ready escalation is period-scale (~2 periods), indifferent to the
453	   minute-scale reordering a shuffle introduces. Two skip rules, both live
454	   reads at pick time:
455	   - **Same-title mutex** (SCENARIOS S15/F6): skip an item whose exact title
456	     (task + qualifier) has another open item in `task:executing` or
457	     `task:agent` — one task, one execution at a time; a fan-out's distinct
458	     qualifiers still parallelize. The skipped item is picked once its twin
459	     converges.
460	   - **The `after` yield** (SCENARIOS S24): skip a scheduled item whose task
461	     declares `after: [T]` while T's standing item is `task:ready`,
462	     `task:executing`, or `task:agent` — yield *while the upstream is live
463	     this cycle*, nothing more. A rolled upstream (blocked until its next
464	     anchor: it declined this cycle) does not block, and neither does one
465	     sitting `needs-human` — a broken upstream must not halt its dependents
466	     indefinitely, the same bound the old exclusive claim drew at three days.
467	     This is deliberately **not** a `Blocked-by` edge: a standing item that
468	     rolls never closes, so wiring `after` as blocked-by-the-item would
469	     starve every dependent of a quiet upstream forever — the one real trap
470	     in the standing-item model, caught in replay (S24).
471	
472	   **The filters are advisory at pick time (F15)**: they read possibly-stale
473	   state, so two executors can pass them simultaneously and claim
474	   *different* items the filters should have serialized — a twin pair, or an
475	   upstream and its dependent. The per-item lease cannot see this (it
476	   protects one item, not one title). So after **winning** a claim, the
477	   executor re-verifies the filters against live state; if a conflicting
478	   item now holds an **earlier** claim (comment order — the same arbiter the
479	   lease trusts), it reverts its own claim to `task:ready` and moves on.
480	   Bounded (one revert per conflict), deterministic (comment order), and
481	   the earlier claim never notices (S32).
482	
483	   Take the first survivor. None → exit quietly.
484	2. **Claim — the verified lease, unchanged in shape** (it earned its keep):
485	   read labels, abandon if `task:ready` is gone or `task:executing` /
486	   `task:agent` / `needs-human` present; swap `task:ready → task:executing` and
487	   post the claim comment (executor id, run URL, UTC time); re-read, earliest
488	   claim comment wins, loser reverts nothing and moves on — it may pick a
489	   *different* item and try again (an executor is code iterating a queue, not a
490	   session sweeping one; the one-session-one-issue rule binds agents, and each
491	   claimed item still gets exactly one agent). Three precisions the
492	   simulator's validation review forced (2026-08-13), each an implicit
493	   assumption made explicit:
494	   - **"Earliest" means lowest comment *id*, never timestamp** — GitHub
495	     comment `created_at` has one-second granularity, so simultaneous claims
496	     tie on time; comment ids are server-assigned and strictly increasing,
497	     a total order the protocol gets for free. Nothing in the lease may
498	     compare runner clocks.
499	   - **The arbiter is episode-scoped (F18)**: earliest claim comment **since
500	     the item last became ready** — the revert/reclaim/re-queue comment is
501	     the episode boundary. Over the item's lifetime, dead claims accumulate
502	     (every reclaim and revert leaves one behind); arbitrating over all of
503	     them makes a *dead* claim outrank every future live claimant, and the
504	     item livelocks through reclaim cycles forever. Caught by the simulator
505	     racing two executors onto a reverted item (S32) — and masked until
506	     then because a single executor beats its own stale claim by id
507	     equality.
508	   - **Letting go of an open item kills your claim (F24)**: the boundary is
509	     a *rule about every path that ends an episode*, not a property of the
510	     three that happened to write a comment. An executor that stops owning
511	     an item without closing it — the roll, every `needs-human` park, and a
512	     claimant that *lost* the arbitration — **strikes its own claim**,
513	     appending the episode marker to the claim comment it already wrote. The
514	     loser matters as much as the winner: its claim is younger than the
515	     winner's, so it survives the winner's own strike and becomes the
516	     earliest claim of the *next* episode, moving the livelock one episode
517	     along rather than removing it. That satisfies the boundary with no new
518	     timeline entry, which is what lets the roll keep its silence (§5); a
519	     marker *comment* there would put one on every declining hourly task,
520	     every hour. Only a claim's author strikes it, so a claim can be
521	     withdrawn but never forged earlier, and comment ids still give the
522	     total order. A successful hand-off does **not** strike — that episode
523	     is live, owned by the session — and a *dead* executor strikes nothing,
524	     which is the case the leash reclaim already covers.
525	   - **The label swap is two API calls, not a CAS** — GitHub has no atomic
526	     label swap. That is fine *because* labels are not the arbiter: they are
527	     visibility and the pick filter; the claim comments arbitrate, so a torn
528	     swap can never mint a second owner. What it *can* do — executor dies
529	     between the remove and the add — is leave an open item with **no state
530	     label at all**, invisible to every rule that filters by state. The
531	     janitor gains the repair (§11): an open work item wearing neither a
532	     `task:*` state nor `needs-human` is off the state machine entirely →
533	     `needs-human` + `task:needs-human-decision`, a human's to look at — which
534	     state it should have had is a judgement about what actually ran.
535	3. **Validate in code**: the body's first line is a legal task path, the file
536	   exists at HEAD, the pack is declared, `task.mjs` parses. Task gone → close,
537	   `task:obsolete`, comment. Malformed → `needs-human` +
538	   `task:needs-human-failure` (possible forgery, a human must see it),
539	   unchanged from today.
540	4. **Evaluate the precondition — the only place it ever runs** (the sketch's
541	   "evaluates preconditions", now literally once). Creation was calendar-only
542	   (§5), so this is not a re-check of anything — it is *the* verdict, over
543	   signals the executor collects for this one task. On **go**: proceed, with
544	   the verdict's Context written into the body as the agent's binding scope.
545	   On **no-go**: a scheduled item **rolls** — `Not-before` stamped with the
546	   task's next anchor, `task:ready → task:blocked`, the reason recorded — and
547	   an ad-hoc item (a manual task's, or qualified — no anchor to roll to, §3)
548	   closes `task:obsolete` with the reason commented (a follow-up whose world
549	   settled on its own, S17). **This amends §12.3's "the precondition is the
550	   only decision point" by re-siting, not weakening it**: still exactly the
551	   precondition deciding, still one decision point — moved from the scheduler
552	   run to the pick — and the work step and the agent still may not skip; the
553	   doctrine's target (later phases inventing "new reasons to skip") is
554	   untouched.

556	   **This stays clean only while preconditions ask task questions, not
557	   calendar ones** (owner's condition, 2026-08-13). "Is there work?" is a
558	   question about the world; "has it been more than a day?" is the scheduler's
559	   own question leaking into a task, and under this model it is doubly wrong —
560	   the item already *carries* its schedule in `Not-before`, so a calendar
561	   precondition would be a second clock disagreeing with the first. Timing
562	   belongs to `frequency`, the anchors, and `Not-before`. The rule is
563	   **advisory** by owner ruling: no mechanical check (the property is not
564	   checkable), and the residual exposure is an item rolled with a calendar
565	   reason in its record — visible, and it costs a cycle, not correctness. The one live offender is resolved by
566	   ruling rather than grandfathered: **baselining's `ageDays > 1` gate is
567	   dropped outright** (owner, 2026-08-13: "the wrong precondition"). Its
568	   precondition becomes the work question alone — is the mount behind canon
569	   head, are migration notes unapplied — with cadence carried by
570	   `frequency: daily-2h` and nothing else. The corpus enters the new mechanism
571	   with zero calendar preconditions.
572	5. **The work step**, Action-side, unchanged contract: subprocess, task dir
573	   cwd, `required_secrets` as env, timeout, `CLAUDINITE_REQUEST_AGENT`
574	   conditional hand-off. **This step is the work, not preparation for it**
575	   (owner correction, 2026-08-15): for most of the fleet it is the whole task —
576	   long-running, crash-prone, PR-creating — and the agent phase is the
577	   sometimes-important judgment minority. The contract key is still spelled
578	   `code_work` (renaming a vendored key is a migration, tracked separately);
579	   the design calls the phase what it is. Three requirements, the first
580	   stated explicitly since SCENARIOS S8/F12:
581	   - **Re-entrant** — a dead executor's claim is reclaimed and the item
582	     re-picked, so the work can run again over its own half-done output (it
583	     already must survive this today, where a scheduler run dying mid-work
584	     leaves the slot due; the contract just never said so).
585	   - **Heartbeat while it runs** (work-as-work review, 2026-08-15): the
586	     executor comments on the item every ~15 minutes during the work step.
587	     The heartbeat is what lets one short global executing leash survive
588	     arbitrarily long work — the leash measures executor *death* (heartbeats
589	     stopped), never work *duration* — and it is the item's visibility during
590	     the hours its timeline would otherwise go dark (§11 has the leash
591	     arithmetic this replaces).
592	   - **The terminal comment is the durable record.** Actions logs expire; the
593	     item is what remains. Whatever ends the item — converge here, or the
594	     agent later — the closing comment carries the `claudinite-task-exec`
595	     record and every artifact the work created (PR links above all). For an
596	     agentless task this comment is the *only* durable trace of the run, which
597	     is what makes it non-optional.
598	
599	   Failure → comment + `needs-human` + a sub-label, `task:executing` removed —
600	   and **the worker chooses which sub-label**. The executor sees an exit code
601	   and nothing else, so it cannot tell a token missing a scope (a person's
602	   five-second fix) from an exception in the worker's own code (an afternoon);
603	   a worker that knows prints `claudinite-needs-human: <kind> — <detail>` on
604	   either stream before exiting non-zero and the park routes on it. Read from
605	   the output rather than a file, because it must survive the SIGKILL at
606	   `code_work_timeout` — output is echoed live, a file written at exit is never
607	   written at all. The last marker wins, so a sweep may revise its verdict as
608	   it works through its targets; no marker parks at `failure`, which is what
609	   every worker written before the marker existed does in every run.
610	
611	   Success, agentless task or no agent requested → converge now: `task:done`,
612	   close, done — the quiet-on-success property survives as a *closed* item
613	   rather than no item, which is the better trade: the run is now visible.
614	   **Unless the payload names an unmerged PR**, which is not a finished run but
615	   a waiting reviewer: that parks at `task:needs-human-approval`, open, and does
616	   not hold the lane.
617	6. **Hand off**: write `### Delivered by code-work` / `### Why the agent is
618	   here` into the body (unchanged shapes), swap `task:executing → task:agent`,
619	   post the hand-off comment carrying a fresh **invocation nonce**, then
620	   **fire the invocation endpoint exactly once** with a payload naming this
621	   issue and that nonce.
622	
623	   **Once per item, ever — and that one decision removes a whole protocol**
624	   (owner, 2026-08-15). An earlier draft retried a timed-out call and, because
625	   a client-side timeout may still have started a session, accepted
626	   at-least-once invocation and paid for it with an agent-side claim lease
627	   (§7) to collapse the duplicates. But a retry is only safe when you know the
628	   first call did nothing, and the timeout is exactly the case where you
629	   cannot know. Declining to retry keeps invocation **at-most-once**, so two
630	   sessions can never arrive at one item and the lease has nothing to collapse.
631	   The nonce survives, earning its keep differently: it proves a fire names
632	   *this* hand-off rather than a stale or replayed one.
633	
634	   Three outcomes, and the third is the whole point:
635	   - **fired** — a session exists; the item is the agent's.
636	   - **refused** (a status came back) — no session, and the cause is a token,
637	     a URL or a routine, which no retry fixes: converge `needs-human` +
638	     `task:needs-human-action` naming it.
639	   - **unanswered** (a timeout, a dropped connection) — the session may or may
640	     not exist, and nothing may guess. The item **stays** `task:agent` with a
641	     comment saying the outcome is unknown; whichever way it went is settled by
642	     a rule that already exists — a session that started converges the item, and
643	     one that never did leaves it silent until the janitor's agent leash (§11)
644	     brings it to triage. No new mechanism, no re-queue that could duplicate.
645	
646	   Either way a lost hand-off is a *synchronous, visible* event at the
647	   executor, not a silently missing label event (this is what retires the
648	   re-arm — §11, and the credential it costs is §12).
649	
650	**An executor run performs one item** — not a configured maximum but the
651	executor's essence (owner, 2026-08-15): claim it, see it through to its
652	settle (roll, close, hand-off, or failure), end. The run's `timeout-minutes`
653	sizes to a single work bound, a platform kill loses at most one item's
654	progress, and self-re-dispatch (§10) chains the rest at ~a minute of spin-up
655	per item. Each item's claim is independently leased, so executor concurrency
656	is safe at any width. The old
657	bound tying the run to its leash — `timeout-minutes` ≤ the executing leash, so
658	the platform killed a hung runner before its claim was reaped — **retires with
659	the heartbeat** (2026-08-15): it capped every run at under an hour, which the
660	work-as-work model cannot accept. The stalled-worker lesson
661	([RESEARCH](RESEARCH.md) §2) is now held by three smaller pieces instead: a
662	*dead* runner stops heartbeating and is reclaimed within ~the leash; a *wedged
663	work subprocess* is killed by the work's own declared timeout (the contract's
664	existing bound), after which the executor converges the failure; and a
665	*reclaimed-but-alive* runner abandons at its next transition, because the
666	executor re-verifies its own lease at every state change (§11). The run's
667	`timeout-minutes` is then sized to the work it may legally do — the largest
668	single work bound it can pick — not to the leash.
669	
670	**Idempotency, honestly (owner concern, 2026-08-13: "I'm not sure we can
671	guarantee all tasks to be idempotent").** Agreed — and the design does not
672	require it. The queue literature's blanket "make handlers idempotent" applies
673	to systems where duplicate *invocations* reach the handler; here the executor
674	claim collapses duplicate pickups **before work starts** (§6.2) and at-most-once
675	invocation means no duplicate ever reaches the agent hop (§6.6), so what tasks
676	must actually tolerate is much narrower:
677	
678	- **The work step must be re-entrant** — a *sequential* re-run after a
679	  crash-and-reclaim (§6.5). That is convergence ("check what exists, continue
680	  from there"), not idempotency, and it is already required of the work today.
681	  Concurrent overlap with a zombie run is excluded by the lease re-verify and
682	  the work's own timeout (above), not asked of the task.
683	- **Re-executed agent work passes through the precondition again** (§6.4),
684	  and the half-run's artifacts are on the item (Delivered section, the
685	  PR-number comments the agent posts as it works — the item is the run's own
686	  inbox/outbox). A re-pick therefore *sees* what already happened and
687	  converges `task:obsolete` instead of redoing it — check-before-act,
688	  carried by the mechanism, not by task-author discipline.
689	- The residual overlap cases are bounded by the **write ceiling**: the worst
690	  historical duplicate produced twin PRs — visible, closeable, never
691	  destructive.
692	
693	And for a task that can promise none of this — a genuinely one-shot side
694	effect (a store submission, an external notification, a payment-shaped
695	action): the contract gains **`on_interrupt: 'requeue' | 'needs-human'`**
696	(default `'requeue'`). Declaring `'needs-human'` makes every recovery path
697	that would re-execute — leash reclaim (§11), the human re-queue lever (§4) —
698	converge to triage instead (`task:needs-human-decision`: whether the
699	interrupted run left anything behind is exactly the choice being handed over):
700	**at-most-once plus a human**. This is the ack-early/ack-late dial every queue exposes, and
701	Celery ships ack-early as its *default* precisely so non-idempotent tasks
702	are never silently re-run ([RESEARCH](RESEARCH.md) §1); here the safe-side
703	default stays `'requeue'` because most of this fleet's tasks are
704	sweep-shaped, and the one-shot minority declares itself. Running
705	more executors — a second workflow instance, a laptop, a k8s job — requires
706	only an issues-scope token; nothing about the queue knows how many exist.

708	## 7. The agent
709	
710	> Amended 2026-08-18 (§16.6): a session that picks up a request item validates the
711	> issue it names as well as the item, runs at the item's `Model:`, and writes the
712	> result back onto that issue when it parks for approval.
713	
714	Today's `executor.md` collapses: the trigger-identification dance
715	(`resolve-dispatch`'s not-mine / scope-mismatch / no-trigger / needs-issue
716	verdicts, the two transports, the no-fallback rule)
717	existed because the session had to *discover* which label event started it. An
718	invoked session is told its item in its prompt — one issue number — and the
719	prompt is written by executor code, not by a human. What survives, verbatim in
720	role: validate the item in code before acting (never trust the prompt more
721	than a label event — re-resolve the task path at HEAD), honor the Context as
722	binding scope, run `task.md` at the declared model with the declared timeout
723	stated plainly, verify the outcome ceiling in code (`verify-outcome`), converge
724	the item (`task:done`, or a park under one of the four sub-labels + comment),
725	print the `claudinite-task-exec` record, capture the session. One session, one
726	item, no queue awareness — unchanged, and now structural: the session never
727	receives a queue, only an item.
728	
729	**The agent does NOT claim** (owner, 2026-08-15 — reversing an earlier draft of
730	this section). A claim lease here would answer "two sessions arrived at one
731	item", and under at-most-once invocation (§6.6) that cannot happen: the endpoint
732	is called once per item and never retried, so there is no second session to
733	arbitrate against. Adding the lease anyway would be machinery maintaining a
734	property the caller already guarantees — and machinery that reads as a licence to
735	retry, which is what would break the guarantee.
736	
737	What the session does instead is **check, not claim**: before touching anything,
738	confirm in code that the item carries `task:agent` and that its newest hand-off
739	comment carries the nonce this fire was given. A mismatch means the fire names a
740	hand-off that is not the current one — a replay, or an episode that has since been
741	reclaimed — and the session stops without touching the item. One comparison, no
742	protocol, and it costs nothing when it passes.
743	
744	The session's instructions are themselves a tracked file
745	([`engine/scheduler/queue/instructions.md`](../../engine/scheduler/queue/instructions.md))
746	that the routine's stored prompt does nothing but point at, so the issue-is-data
747	posture holds at this hop too: the payload names an item, and every instruction
748	comes from a file under review.

750	## 8. Urgency and forcing — creating or waking an item is the whole mechanism
751	
752	- **Urgent** work is an item with `task:urgent`: picked first, and the
753	  `labeled` event gives it executor latency of one spin-up. Nothing else is
754	  special about it.
755	- **Forcing a scheduled task is waking its standing item** (owner model,
756	  2026-08-13). The item exists (§5), so force = strip `task:blocked` **and
757	  add `task:ready`**, clear `Not-before`, optionally add `task:urgent` — the
758	  same lever as the human re-queue (§4), which is no accident: "run this
759	  now" and "retry this now" are the same operation on the same object.
760	  `task:ready` is not bookkeeping: `pickOrder` (§6.1) admits on that label
761	  alone, so an item merely stripped of `task:blocked` wears no state any
762	  executor selects on, and the run reports `nothing ready to pick up` —
763	  indistinguishable from a healthy idle run. **When the standing item does
764	  not exist, forcing MINTS it** — a completed task closes its item and the
765	  next appears only at its anchor, so for most of a daily task's day there
766	  is nothing to wake, and refusing there would make a fleet-wide converge
767	  lever fail on most members most of the time. The minted item is an
768	  ordinary standing item: it consumes the current
769	  occurrence (so the tick does not create a second one beside it) and leaves
770	  the next anchor's alone. Cross-repo, the enforcer does not perform any of
771	  this itself; it dispatches the member's scheduler with a `wake` input and
772	  the member's own tick applies the recipe (§14). The executor evaluates the
773	  precondition at pick like always; a no-go rolls the item again with the
774	  reason on record, so a force that finds no work *says so* where the
775	  operator will read it. Truly unconditional force: say so in a Context line
776	  the task's precondition honors — but the default stands that even forced
777	  work is admitted by code. *(Deliberate divergence from #515's "forcing
778	  never consults the task"; its motivating case — the slot gate running
779	  before preconditions made mid-day forcing unreachable — does not exist
780	  here: nothing runs before the pick.)*
781	- **Forcing ad-hoc work is creating an item**: parameterized runs, `manual`
782	  tasks, fan-out targets. The CLI/composite (`create-work-item <pack>/<task>
783	  [--urgent] [--context …] [--supersedes #N]`) writes the generic "forced by
784	  hand — no precondition asserts there is work" Context; `--supersedes`
785	  additionally closes a named errored item as superseded by this retry. The
786	  CLI warns when an open same-title item exists — the pick-time mutex (§6.1)
787	  means the new item queues behind it, and the operator should know they are
788	  queueing, not jumping (SCENARIOS S15/F6). `FORCE_TASKS`, the
789	  forced-verdict path, the `~f` marker and the watermark exclusion all
790	  reduce to these two levers.
791	- **Cancelling one executor run means "move on", and the mechanism already
792	  reads it that way** (owner, 2026-08-16). A single cancellation is
793	  indistinguishable from a crash: the failure continuation (§10) keeps the
794	  train moving, and the cancelled run's item is freed by the leash. What a
795	  single cancellation can *never* mean is "stop the system" — the tick and
796	  events keep spawning runs — so that intent gets its own lever:
797	- **Suspending the whole queue is `CLAUDINITE_TASKS_SUSPEND_ALL`** (owner,
798	  2026-08-16): a repo Actions **variable** (`vars.*`, stamped into each
799	  workflow's env by the wiring — settable in the UI or over the API, **no
800	  commit**), which every Claudinite workflow — tick and executor alike —
801	  checks as its *first act* and, when true, exits cleanly having fired
802	  nothing. The train parks at most one hop after suspension (an already
803	  in-flight continuation may fire one re-dispatch; that fresh run sees the
804	  variable and parks). Suspension gates workflow *starts* only: in-flight
805	  runs and agent sessions finish on their own — cancel those by hand if the
806	  hold is urgent — and items freeze exactly where they are, no labels
807	  touched, which is what makes the hold stateless. This is not dormancy:
808	  `dormant` is a *declared standing state* in tracked config, a commit,
809	  read by the same gates; the suspend variable is the instant, out-of-band
810	  operational hold. (S37.)
811	- **Resuming is clearing the variable — recovery needs no lever of its own.**
812	  The next cron tick performs the entire self-heal unaided: its reclaim job
813	  frees the claims of runs killed during the hold (their heartbeats long
814	  silent), its readiness job wakes whatever came due, and its drain picks the
815	  queue back up. An operator who won't wait the ≤1h dispatches the
816	  **scheduler** workflow by hand — the tick-plus-drain pair, *not* the bare
817	  executor, whose run would drain ready items but skip the reclaim/ready
818	  half that makes resume complete. (S38.)
819	- **`manual` tasks** are simply tasks the tick never instantiates: their items
820	  are only ever created by hand or by other tasks. The frequency token
821	  survives; the special-case slot resolution for it dies.
822	- **Fan-out across repos** is the enforcer creating one item per member repo
823	  (urgent when the pass is urgent) instead of firing member schedulers with
824	  `FORCE_TASKS` — same write-gated surface, and the fan-in below gives the
825	  enforcer something it never had: a status. Nothing about it is a "fleet
826	  mechanism": it is a task creating items, and if its work needs wider reach
827	  than the repo's ordinary sessions have, it names a wider invocation endpoint
828	  (§12).

830	## 9. Follow-ups, ordering, fan-in — the dependency fields
831	
832	`Blocked-by: #N[, #M…]` and `Not-before: <ISO instant>` on an item, evaluated
833	by the tick (§5). Three patterns fall out, all from the sketch:
834	
835	- **Follow-up validation.** A task whose run delivered something long-running
836	  (a store submission, an armed auto-merge, a real-world change that settles
837	  over days) closes `task:done` and creates its own follow-up item:
838	  `Blocked-by: #<this item>` (satisfied the moment this item closes) +
839	  `Not-before: <now + settle time>`. The tick readies it when the time passes;
840	  an executor then re-runs its precondition — which checks whether the world
841	  actually settled — and the item either runs, or closes obsolete because
842	  everything landed on its own. The "will anyone check tomorrow?" gap closes
843	  with machinery that is just two body fields.
844	- **Ordering, declared — the exclusive claim retires.** A task may declare
845	  `after: ['basics/baselining']` in `task.mjs`, and it compiles to the
846	  **pick-time yield** (§6.1), *not* to a `Blocked-by` edge: the executor
847	  skips the dependent while the upstream's standing item is live
848	  (ready/executing/agent) this cycle, and picks it the moment the upstream
849	  converges — or rolls. The distinction is load-bearing under the
850	  standing-item model: `Blocked-by` requires the blocker *closed*, and a
851	  standing item that rolls never closes, so wiring `after` as blocked-by
852	  would starve every dependent of a quiet upstream forever (S24 — the one
853	  trap found replaying the model). As a yield: on the late-fire night all
854	  chain items are created together, baselining runs first, extract and
855	  promote follow *the same night* in order; on the routine night where
856	  baselining's precondition declines and its item rolls, extract is pickable
857	  a minute later. Nothing is spent, no task claims a run, and the engine
858	  still never knows what baselining is — `after` names a task id, and the
859	  pick filter reads item states, generically. §12's exclusive-claim
860	  machinery (and its stated throughput cost) deletes. `Blocked-by` remains
861	  the right edge for what it is: dependencies on items that *terminate*
862	  (follow-ups, fan-ins).
863	- **Fan-out with a fan-in.** Fanning out is creating N items (§8). The fan-in
864	  is one more item — the status/aggregation task — created `Blocked-by` all N.
865	  It readies only when every child converged, and its precondition/work step read
866	  the children's outcome labels to report or escalate. "Getting the status of
867	  a fan-out" stops being a bespoke sweep and becomes an ordinary task whose
868	  edges the tick already evaluates.
869	
870	**Readiness has a second site: whoever closes an item re-checks its dependents
871	in code** (F1, reopened by the owner 2026-08-15 — reversing the 2026-08-13
872	decline, and amending §15.8's "dependency readiness is the tick's alone" in
873	siting, not in principle). On closing an item, the executor or agent doing the
874	closing evaluates every open `task:blocked` item naming it: `Blocked-by` all
875	closed and `Not-before` passed flips the dependent to `task:ready`, and a
876	drain follows — so a chain link or a fan-in proceeds within minutes of its
877	upstream converging instead of waiting out the tick. What changed since the
878	decline: under the work-as-work model the ~1h/link quantization stacks on
879	drain occupancy, so a three-link chain on a busy morning trailed into the
880	afternoon. The tick's readiness job stays exactly as it was, as the backstop —
881	a close by hand runs no engine code, and a missed re-check costs a tick of
882	latency, never correctness (SCENARIOS S33, and S4's tightened chain timing).
883	
884	Native GitHub issue dependencies (blocked-by/blocking — GA since Aug 2025,
885	API- and webhook-supported) and sub-issues *mirror* these fields: the tick
886	writes the native edge alongside the body field, buying the dependency UI for
887	free ([RESEARCH](RESEARCH.md) §2). The body fields remain the truth the tick
888	parses — they are portable to any tracker with issues, labels, and comments,
889	which is the platform-agnosticism the sketch asks for. One vendored module owns
890	parse/serialize of the two fields; nothing else touches them.
891	
892	Cycles: the tick readies nothing in a `Blocked-by` cycle, forever, and the
893	stale escalation (§11) surfaces it as `needs-human` + `task:needs-human-action` after ~2 periods — the
894	same convergence-not-prevention posture as the rest of the system. The tick
895	does not attempt cycle detection; the janitor's health review may.

897	## 10. Capacity and platform-agnosticism
898	
899	The default deployment stays one vendored cron workflow — the repo's only
900	cron, rule unchanged — containing the tick job and a drain (the tick runs
901	first; the executor drains what it created, which keeps the common case's
902	latency at zero even without events). Event triggers (`task:ready` labeled)
903	give urgent and hand-created items sub-minute pickup — with one platform fact
904	worth knowing: a label written by a workflow's own `GITHUB_TOKEN` emits no
905	triggering event (GitHub's recursion guard), so events only ever come from
906	*foreign* tokens — a human, a CLI on a PAT, an agent session. The drain being
907	in-run is what makes that harmless; it is the structural delivery, events the
908	sugar.
909	
910	**The capacity model, honestly** (work-as-work review, 2026-08-15): the work
911	step is the work, so throughput is run *occupancy* — one run, one item, and
912	the queue drains as a chain of runs. The CCR sessions runs hand off
913	parallelize for free; the executor-side work does not. So executor width is
914	the primary capacity parameter, not a garnish: scale with a matrix width for
915	parallel executor jobs, or with executors outside Actions entirely — the
916	contract is "issue read/write plus the repo checkout at HEAD", so a runner
917	anywhere with a token qualifies. The chain itself is **self-re-dispatch**:
918	`workflow_dispatch` is one of the two event types a `GITHUB_TOKEN` *can*
919	fire, so a run that ends with ready items left re-dispatches the executor
920	workflow and a fresh run continues.
921	One fairness note, accepted at today's scale: the randomized pick (§6.1)
922	removes any *systematic* head domination, but a heavy item still occupies its
923	run for the full work bound while light tasks wait out the chain — a sentence
924	here rather than machinery, until it is measured.
925	
926	**What starts an executor run is an enumerable list, and each cause is on the
927	record** (2026-08-15, and the sim asserts it — S34): (1) **the tick's own
928	drain job** — the guaranteed delivery, started by the cron workflow's job
929	graph (`needs: tick`), no event involved; (2) **a `task:ready`/`task:urgent`
930	label event** — foreign tokens only, the latency sugar; (3) **the close-time
931	drain** — whoever converges an item triggers a drain when anything is
932	pickable after its readiness re-check (§9); (4) **self-re-dispatch** — a run
933	that ends its one item with others still pickable dispatches a fresh run;
934	(5) **the failure continuation** — a run that dies (crash, timeout,
935	cancellation, runner loss) never reaches its re-dispatch, so the executor
936	workflow carries a second job, `needs: execute` with `if: failure() ||
937	cancelled()`, which the platform runs on a fresh runner and whose one step
938	re-dispatches — a dead run stalls the train by ~a minute, not until the next
939	cron fire (S36). Causes 3–5 ride `workflow_dispatch`, which the default
940	`GITHUB_TOKEN` *is* permitted to fire — the explicit exemption in the same
941	recursion guard that suppresses its label events — so no wider credential is
942	involved.
